title: Organic Chemistry
lines: Organic chemistry has the most chemistry questions in USAT. They ask for IUPAC names, functional groups, isomers, the type of a reaction and its product, simple tests that tell compounds apart, and facts about biomolecules and polymers. Learn the reaction type of each family: that one fact predicts most products.
## Basics
- Carbon forms four bonds and links to itself in chains and rings (catenation), giving millions of compounds.
- A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula; neighbouring members differ by CH₂. Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
| Family | Group | Name ending | Example
| Alcohol | –OH | -ol | ethanol C₂H₅OH
| Aldehyde | –CHO | -al | ethanal CH₃CHO
| Ketone | C=O in the chain | -one | propanone CH₃COCH₃
| Carboxylic acid | –COOH | -oic acid | ethanoic acid CH₃COOH
| Ester | –COOR | -oate | ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOC₂H₅
| Amine | –NH₂ | -amine | ethylamine C₂H₅NH₂
- IUPAC naming: find the longest chain containing the main group, number it from the end nearer that group, then list side chains as prefixes with their positions.
> Example 1. Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH.
> The longest chain holding the OH has three carbons (propanol); number from the OH end: OH on C-1, methyl on C-2. The name is 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
## Isomerism

- Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures: chain (butane and 2-methylpropane), position (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol) and functional group (ethanol and methoxymethane).
- Geometric (cis-trans) isomers need a C=C with two different groups on each carbon, such as but-2-ene.
- Optical isomers contain a chiral carbon: one carrying four different groups, as in lactic acid.
- Counts worth knowing: C₄H₁₀ has 2 isomers, C₅H₁₂ has 3, and C₄H₁₀O has 4 alcohols.
## Reaction types
- Homolytic bond fission gives free radicals; heterolytic fission gives ions.
- Electrophiles seek electrons (H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br⁺); nucleophiles donate a lone pair (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O).
| Family | Typical reaction
| Alkanes | free-radical substitution (Cl₂ in light)
| Alkenes, alkynes | electrophilic addition
| Benzene | electrophilic substitution
| Alkyl halides | nucleophilic substitution or elimination
| Aldehydes, ketones | nucleophilic addition
## Hydrocarbons
- Alkenes decolourise bromine water and cold alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's test); alkanes do not.
- Markovnikov's rule: when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, H goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens. With peroxide, HBr adds the other way.
- Ethyne is made from calcium carbide and water. Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic and give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate.
- Benzene has six equal C–C bonds and a delocalised π cloud, so it prefers substitution to addition. Nitration uses concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ (electrophile NO₂⁺); halogenation needs FeBr₃ or AlCl₃.
- Groups such as –OH, –NH₂ and –CH₃ direct new groups to the ortho and para positions; –NO₂, –CHO and –COOH direct to meta.
> Example 2. Give the main product when HBr adds to propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.
> H goes to the end CH₂ carbon (it already has more H); Br goes to the middle carbon. The product is 2-bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃.
## Functional group chemistry
- Alkyl halides: aqueous KOH substitutes to give an alcohol; alcoholic KOH eliminates to give an alkene. SN1 suits tertiary halides, SN2 primary ones.
- Alcohols: primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes and then acids; secondary to ketones; tertiary resist oxidation. Phenol is more acidic than ethanol and gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃.
- Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's solution (red precipitate); ketones do not. Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH.
- The iodoform test (yellow CHI₃) is positive for methyl ketones, ethanal, ethanol and propan-2-ol.
- Carboxylic acids fizz with NaHCO₃, releasing CO₂, and react with alcohols to give esters. Esters smell fruity; alkaline hydrolysis of fats is saponification.
- Amines are weak bases; aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia, and phenylamine is weaker.
> Example 3. Which test distinguishes ethanal from propanone?
> Tollens' reagent: ethanal gives a silver mirror, propanone does not. The iodoform test fails here, because both compounds give it.
## Biomolecules
- Carbohydrates: glucose (an aldohexose) and fructose (a ketohexose) are both C₆H₁₂O₆. Sucrose is glucose + fructose and is non-reducing. Starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose.
- Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–). Amino acids exist as zwitterions; glycine is the only common one without a chiral carbon.
- Lipids: fats and oils are esters of glycerol with fatty acids (triglycerides). Oils are hydrogenated with a nickel catalyst to make ghee.
- Nucleic acids: DNA bases pair A with T and G with C; RNA has uracil in place of thymine. Enzymes are protein catalysts denatured by heat.
## Polymers
- Addition polymers form from alkene monomers with nothing lost: polythene (ethene), PVC (chloroethene), Teflon (tetrafluoroethene), polystyrene (phenylethene).
- Condensation polymers lose a small molecule such as water at each link: nylon-6,6 (from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid) and terylene (a polyester).
- Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene).
> Example 4. A sample of polythene has a molar mass of 28,000 g/mol. How many ethene units does each chain contain?
> Ethene C₂H₄ has M = 28, so the number of units = 28,000 ÷ 28 = 1,000.
! Ester names start with the alcohol part: CH₃COOC₂H₅ is ethyl ethanoate, not ethanoyl ethyl or ethyl methanoate.
! A tertiary alcohol is not oxidised by acidified dichromate; the orange colour stays.
! Cis-trans isomerism is impossible if one carbon of the C=C carries two identical groups, as in propene.
## Quick check
- General formula of alkynes? (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂)
- Reaction type of benzene with nitric acid? (electrophilic substitution)
- Monomer of PVC? (chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl)
- Which gives a silver mirror, an aldehyde or a ketone? (an aldehyde)
- Bond joining amino acids in a protein? (peptide bond)
